Red flags of dubious claims: miracle cures, quick fixes, one-food answers, and 'they don't want you to know' conspiracy framing, each with an original fictional example

claims.claim: A nutrition claim is any statement about what a food, beverage, or dietary supplement does for the body or for health; this working definition is built from how the FDA categorizes label claims (health claims, structure/function claims, nutrient content claims) and how the FTC treats objective statements in advertising.

Anyone can make a nutrition claim: companies, influencers, websites, and even actors hired to appear as satisfied customers; being able to state something is not evidence that it is true, so a claim is not the same as evidence.

Common red flags in nutrition claims include miracle cures, quick fixes, one product claimed to fix many unrelated problems, and 'they don't want you to know' conspiracy framing; MedlinePlus warns that if it sounds too good to be true, it is probably a scam, and no one product can treat or cure many different illnesses.

To check a nutrition claim, ask who is saying it and what their purpose is, what evidence supports it, and who funded it; MedlinePlus's evaluation questions cover who runs the site, whether the purpose is to inform or sell, who pays, whether the information is based on research, and whether it cites sources and dates.

Reliable nutrition information is generally found at federal government agencies (FDA, USDA, NIH), medical schools and universities, and large professional or nonprofit organizations such as the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and the American Heart Association.

In the United States, dietary supplements do not need FDA approval before they are marketed, and structure/function claims (statements about effects on a structure or function of the body) are not approved or pre-evaluated by the FDA; the manufacturer must have substantiation that the claim is truthful and not misleading, and the label must carry a disclaimer stating the FDA has not evaluated the claim and the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.

FTC law requires advertising to be truthful and not misleading, and claims about the health benefits or safety of foods, dietary supplements, and other health products require adequate substantiation, described as competent and reliable scientific evidence.

'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' is a maxim popularized by science communicator Carl Sagan (Broca's Brain, 1979; Cosmos, 1980) and serves as the honest reality check for evaluating nutrition claims.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does 'natural,' 'ancient,' or 'secret' wording indicate a product is safe or effective?
positions: Marketers imply that natural or ancient remedies are inherently safe and effective
NIH ODS: the term 'natural' does not always mean safe, and some botanical products can harm the liver
MedlinePlus lists 'natural cure,' 'ancient remedy,' and 'secret ingredient' among health-fraud phrases
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Where an ingredient comes from or how it is described says nothing about whether it works or is safe; wording is not evidence, so claims built on these words get extra scrutiny.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are customer testimonials proof that a product works?
positions: Advertisers present personal success stories as proof of effectiveness
FTC: testimonials do not substitute for substantiation; ads using them must reflect the results a typical consumer can expect, and 'results not typical' disclaimers do not cure deception
MedlinePlus lists testimonials by 'real people' or actors as a red flag
conflictingEvidence.resolution: A testimonial is one person's story, not evidence; claims need research that is conducted and reviewed by experts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How does a structure/function claim differ from a disease claim on a supplement label?
positions: Structure/function claims describe effects on a structure or function of the body and need no FDA preapproval, but require substantiation and a disclaimer
A product represented explicitly or implicitly as treating, curing, or preventing a specific disease meets the definition of a drug
The FTC notes that structure/function wording can still imply a disease benefit depending on context and imagery
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Read the exact wording and the disclaimer; disease claims turn a supplement into a drug claim under U.S. law, and implied disease claims still need substantiation.

sourceRecords.title: Questions and Answers on Dietary Supplements
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: FDA does not approve dietary supplements or their labeling before marketing; structure/function claims describe the role of a nutrient or dietary ingredient intended to affect the structure or function of the body, are not approved or pre-evaluated by FDA, require manufacturer substantiation, and must carry the disclaimer that FDA has not evaluated the claim and the product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease; a product represented as treating/curing a disease meets the definition of a drug; FTC regulates supplement advertising. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: FDA 101: Dietary Supplements
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: FDA does not have authority to approve dietary supplements for safety and effectiveness or to approve their labeling before sale; a product intended to treat, prevent, cure, or alleviate symptoms of a disease is a drug; FDA's supplement role is largely postmarket. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Health Fraud
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: health fraud products have not been proven effective; 'if it sounds too good to be true, it's probably a scam'; red flags include testimonials by 'real people' or actors, one product claimed to treat many unrelated diseases, conspiracy framing ('the cure our government and Big Pharma don't want you to know about'), and phrases such as miracle cure, quick fix, natural cure, ancient remedy, secret ingredient, and scientific breakthrough. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Evaluating Health Information
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: good health information is found on sites run by federal government agencies, medical schools, and large professional or nonprofit organizations; evaluation questions include who runs the site, the site's purpose (inform vs. sell), who pays for it (ads should be marked; business-funded info may favor that business), whether information is balanced and based on research, and whether sources and dates are given. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Dietary Supplements: What You Need to Know (Fact Sheet for Consumers)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: medicines must be approved by FDA before sale but supplements do not require this approval; supplement companies are responsible for having evidence that products are safe and label claims are truthful and not misleading; 'natural' does not always mean safe. Facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: Health Products Compliance Guidance
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: advertising must be truthful and not misleading; advertisers must have adequate substantiation for all objective product claims; health-benefit claims about foods, dietary supplements, drugs, and other health products require substantiation in the form of competent and reliable scientific evidence; testimonials must reflect typical results. Facts synthesized in original wording.
